rationale: D15: a class whose HEAD is decorated by a macro is still a class, and must be published as one. tree-sitter-cpp cannot read `class GTEST_API_ UnitTestImpl { ... };` and does not merely decline it — it recovers the whole declaration as a FUNCTION, with the specifier's `name` field holding the MACRO (`type_identifier GTEST_API_`), the real class name sitting beside it as a bare sibling `identifier`, and the class body as the function's `compound_statement`. Because the specifier then carries no body of its own, the forward-declaration rule declines it and THE CLASS IS NEVER PUBLISHED. Two things follow. The bare sibling reads as a function declarator, so the class's own name is published as a function. And the out-of-line definitions of that class's members (`Widget::reset() { ... }`) resolve their owner by the `Widget::` qualifier to whichever `Widget` symbol exists — the CONSTRUCTOR, which shares the class's name, so every member's body is owned by a one-line constructor declaration. MEASURED at HEAD: across the five pinned C++ corpora, 93 macro-decorated class declarations, 5 published, 88 lost; and in fmt/test/gtest/gmock-gtest-all.cc `UnitTestImpl` was published at `902-902`, the constructor's own declaration line, while owning 91 edges spread over lines 902-1354. After the fix all 93 publish, and `UnitTestImpl` spans `900-1355` with every one of those 91 edges inside it. What HEAD published for this very file, and what every row below pins against: `UnitTestImpl` as a FUNCTION at `27-27`, `value` as a function with no owner, `cached_` as a variable with no owner, and `Reporter` not published at all. `Reporter` is a STRUCT spelling, included because gtest, abseil and the catch2 self-test each spell their decorated classes both ways and a rule that recognised only `class` would half-fix the corpus. THE D11 CONTROL is the `class Widget f();` block and it is the reason the all-caps test is load-bearing rather than tidy: that member also has a class_specifier as the `type` field of a function_definition, and its compound_statement is a body too, so a detector that stopped at 'a specifier with no body of its own' would swallow it, publish a second class named `Widget`, and re-own the body. The two shapes differ exactly as the gate states them — there the specifier's `name` is `Widget`, a class name rather than a macro spelling, and `f` sits inside a `function_declarator` rather than as a bare sibling. `thing_lowercase` pins the negative direction again from the other side: a lowercase specifier name is not a macro spelling, so a detector loosened to any bodyless specifier is caught even when the sibling identifier happens to look like a name. `Plain` is the plain-class control, whose members were already owned correctly at HEAD.
